title: Nonreversible Gauge Fields in Fokker--Planck Dynamics: Supersymmetric Hamiltonians and Learned Finite Forces
summary: We formulate stationary-density-preserving nonreversible perturbations of Fokker--Planck dynamics as gauge fields that deform relaxation spectra while leaving the invariant state fixed. When detailed balance holds, a similarity transformation maps the reversible Fokker--Planck operator to a Witten-Laplacian-type supersymmetric Hamiltonian; nonreversible gauges then appear as non-Hermitian perturbations that preserve the zero mode but modify the excited spectrum. This operator viewpoint gives a common language for relaxation gaps, circulating probability currents, hypocoercive acceleration, and finite control costs. We represent admissible gauge currents by antisymmetric tensor fields and identify the detailed-balance-violating Ohzeki--Ichiki force as a constant symplectic example whose infinite-strength limit is Hamiltonian dynamics. The continuous-time spectral gap alone does not select a finite gauge strength, so we introduce a finite-time regularized objective and an actor--critic procedure for learning the gauge. An exactly solvable anisotropic Gaussian Ornstein--Uhlenbeck benchmark separates the spectral transition from the finite-time optimum and shows that the learned gauge recovers the Lyapunov-equation optimum. A double-well benchmark then illustrates the same constrained selection in a nonconvex metastable landscape. Stochastic gradient methods enter this framework as physically relevant Fokker--Planck systems: mini-batch noise acts as an effective diffusion tensor, and adaptive methods such as Adam correspond to metric choices with possible nonequilibrium currents.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates nonreversible perturbations of Fokker-Planck dynamics as gauge fields that preserve the stationary distribution, linking them to supersymmetric Hamiltonians, hypocoercive acceleration, and optimal control; it introduces a finite-time regularized objective and actor-critic learning to select the gauge, demonstrates on Gaussian and double-well benchmarks, and connects the framework to stochastic gradient methods like Adam.
AI.motivation: To provide a unified operator-theoretic framework for nonreversible perturbations that preserve the stationary density of Fokker-Planck dynamics, enabling systematic analysis of relaxation gaps, probability currents, hypocoercivity, and control costs.
AI.method: The paper represents admissible gauge currents via antisymmetric tensor fields, identifies the Ohzeki-Ichiki force as a constant symplectic example, introduces a finite-time regularized objective for gauge selection, and develops an actor-critic learning procedure. Analysis is conducted on anisotropic Gaussian Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and double-well benchmarks.
AI.result: The spectral gap alone does not uniquely determine finite gauge strength; the finite-time regularized objective selects a unique optimum, which for the Gaussian case matches the Lyapunov-equation optimum. The double-well benchmark confirms constrained selection in metastable landscapes. The framework also reveals that mini-batch noise acts as an effective diffusion tensor and Adam corresponds to specific metric choices with nonequilibrium currents.
AI.conclusion: Nonreversible gauge perturbations provide a principled way to accelerate relaxation while preserving the invariant measure, with gauge selection naturally regularized by finite-time objectives. The framework unifies hypocoercivity, optimal control, and stochastic optimization methods under a common operator-theoretic language.

title: Reply to "Interpreting Bohm quantum potentials in `Computing quantum waves exactly from classical action'"
comment: Comment on arXiv:2605.20443, 3 pages, no figures
summary: The recent arXiv posting arXiv:2605.20443 by Lohmiller and Slotine attempts to address the omission of the Bohm quantum potential in their proposed exact equivalence between classical action and the Schrödinger equation. They introduce a position-dependent time transformation to argue that the spatial derivatives of the probability density amplitude vanish for the Feynman kernel. A rigorous mathematical examination of this transformation reveals a violation of the multivariable chain rule. The spatial derivatives do not vanish in the physical reference frame. The mathematical framework presented by the authors remains identical to the well-established semiclassical Van Vleck propagator, which is exact exclusively for quadratic potentials.

AI.tldr: This analysis refutes Lohmiller and Slotine's claim of an exact equivalence between classical action and the Schrödinger equation by exposing a chain rule violation in their position-dependent time transformation. Their framework reduces to the Van Vleck propagator, which is exact only for quadratic potentials.
AI.motivation: To address the omission of the Bohm quantum potential in Lohmiller and Slotine's proposed exact equivalence between classical action and the Schrödinger equation.
AI.method: Rigorous mathematical examination of the position-dependent time transformation introduced by Lohmiller and Slotine, specifically analyzing multivariable chain rule compliance and comparing with the Van Vleck propagator.
AI.result: The transformation violates the multivariable chain rule; spatial derivatives of the probability density amplitude do not vanish in the physical reference frame. Their framework is identical to the semiclassical Van Vleck propagator, exact only for quadratic potentials.
AI.conclusion: Lohmiller and Slotine's claimed exact equivalence is mathematically invalid; their result reduces to a well-known semiclassical approximation.

title: Programmable spectral symmetries in an anisotropic quantum Rabi simulator
summary: The quantum Rabi model captures fundamental aspects of light--matter interaction, where symmetry dictates both spectra and dynamics. Over the past years, experiments have explored many of its nonperturbative properties, but have mostly focused on the isotropic limit, where rotating and counterrotating processes are locked together, leaving the broader symmetry landscape largely unexplored. Here we realize a programmable anisotropic quantum Rabi model in a superconducting processor, with independent control of the rotating and counterrotating couplings $(g_1,g_2)$ and of a transverse bias $\varepsilon$. Continuous anisotropy tuning, combined with a duality mapping, gives access to the full parameter space from the Jaynes-Cummings to the anti-Jaynes-Cummings limits. In the deep-strong-coupling regime, we show that anisotropy reconstructs the spectrum and turns complete collapse-revival dynamics into incomplete revivals even near degeneracy. With adiabatic state preparation and joint tomography, we resolve an anisotropy-induced ground-state parity switch, a crossing that has no analogue in the isotropic model. We further observe selective tunnelling associated with hidden symmetry in biased Rabi models and track its anisotropic displacement within the same device. These results establish a controllable route to engineering nonperturbative light--matter Hamiltonians, where symmetry, spectrum, and dynamics can be programmed independently.

AI.tldr: The authors realize a programmable anisotropic quantum Rabi model in a superconducting processor with independent control of rotating and counterrotating couplings, demonstrating anisotropy-induced spectral reconstruction, incomplete collapse-revival dynamics, ground-state parity switches, and selective tunnelling from hidden symmetry across the full Jaynes-Cummings to anti-Jaynes-Cummings parameter space.
AI.motivation: To explore the broader symmetry landscape of the quantum Rabi model beyond the isotropic limit, where rotating and counterrotating processes are locked together, by achieving independent programmable control of these couplings.
AI.method: A programmable superconducting processor implementing an anisotropic quantum Rabi model with independent control of rotating coupling g1, counterrotating coupling g2, and transverse bias ε, using continuous anisotropy tuning combined with a duality mapping to access the full parameter space.
AI.result: Demonstrated that anisotropy reconstructs the spectrum and turns complete collapse-revival dynamics into incomplete revivals; observed an anisotropy-induced ground-state parity switch with no isotropic analogue; tracked selective tunnelling associated with hidden symmetry in biased Rabi models.
AI.conclusion: These results establish a controllable route to engineering nonperturbative light-matter Hamiltonians where symmetry, spectrum, and dynamics can be programmed independently.

title: Frustrated superradiant phases in one- and two-dimensional lattices
summary: Understanding how frustration and symmetry breaking shape collective behavior is a central problem in quantum many-body systems. In this work, we investigate this problem in large one- and two-dimensional arrays of coupled Dicke models on a periodic lattice, where strong light-matter coupling gives rise to a superradiant phase and competition between neighboring order parameters induces spontaneous translational symmetry breaking. Such Dicke lattice models constitute a fundamentally new class of quantum many-body systems, as they simultaneously realize the thermodynamic limit associated with the lattice size and an intrinsic thermodynamic limit arising from collective on-site interactions with quantum emitters. We show that frustration drives photonic density-wave ordering, and that the resulting broken periodicity can be predicted from the excitation spectrum of the symmetric phase, without requiring computationally prohibitive thermodynamic energy minimization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an emergent Nambu-Goldstone mode arises near the critical point in a one-dimensional chain despite the presence of only discrete symmetry, and uncover the mechanism that enables this otherwise forbidden gapless excitation. We also find quasi-periodic ordering in the superradiant phase, reminiscent of quasicrystals, and demonstrate that synthetic magnetic flux provides a powerful knob to control the nature of translational symmetry breaking. Our results establish a new direction in quantum many-body physics where the coexistence of local and global thermodynamic limits gives rise to unconventional symmetry breaking and emergent collective behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates frustration and symmetry breaking in large coupled Dicke lattice models, revealing photonic density-wave ordering, emergent Nambu-Goldstone modes in 1D despite discrete symmetry, quasi-periodic ordering in the superradiant phase, and synthetic magnetic flux control of translational symmetry breaking.
AI.motivation: To understand how frustration and symmetry breaking shape collective behavior in quantum many-body systems, specifically in coupled Dicke lattice models where both local (on-site) and global (lattice) thermodynamic limits coexist.
AI.method: The study analyzes large one- and two-dimensional periodic arrays of coupled Dicke models with strong light-matter coupling, using excitation spectrum analysis of the symmetric phase to predict broken periodicity without thermodynamic energy minimization.
AI.result: Frustration drives photonic density-wave ordering; broken periodicity can be predicted from the symmetric phase excitation spectrum; an emergent Nambu-Goldstone mode appears near the critical point in 1D despite only discrete symmetry; quasi-periodic ordering reminiscent of quasicrystals occurs; synthetic magnetic flux controls translational symmetry breaking.
AI.conclusion: Dicke lattices constitute a new class of quantum many-body systems where coexisting local and global thermodynamic limits yield unconventional symmetry breaking and emergent collective behavior, opening a new direction in quantum many-body physics.

title: Emergent Self-Similar Quantum Revivals in Spiral Drives
summary: We uncover a distinct form of nonequilibrium temporal order: self-similar quantum revivals in a many-body system driven by quasiperiodic spiral kicks, where the system recurrently returns close to its initial state at a hierarchically nested sequence of times. We demonstrate that both the fidelity and entanglement entropy exhibit this self-similar temporal structure. It originates from an emergent dynamical attractor, which we identify, such that all momentum modes eventually fall into the same closed orbits at self-similar times. We analytically justify this behavior and show that, for special momentum modes, this attractor arises as a consequence of a generalized spin echo process, and more generally we prove its existence using quasiperiodic SU(2) cocycles. Interestingly, the dynamics between consecutive revivals supports either volume- or area-law entanglement scaling, tunable via the driving parameters. In the presence of integrability-breaking perturbations, the system eventually heats up, but a long-lived prethermal regime with algebraically tunable lifetime occurs before heating sets in. Our results establish self-similar quantum revivals as a new paradigm for nonequilibrium quantum matter and provide a realistic route for its observation in current quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: Self-similar quantum revivals—a hierarchical recurrence of the system close to its initial state—emerge in a many-body system under quasiperiodic spiral kicks, driven by an identified dynamical attractor. The phenomenon is analytically justified via generalized spin echo and quasiperiodic SU(2) cocycles, exhibits tunable entanglement scaling, and features a long-lived prethermal regime before eventual heating.
AI.motivation: To discover and characterize a new form of nonequilibrium temporal order—self-similar quantum revivals—in driven many-body systems, and to establish its physical origin and observable signatures.
AI.method: Quasiperiodic spiral driving of a many-body system; analysis of fidelity and entanglement entropy; identification of a dynamical attractor where all momentum modes fall into closed self-similar orbits; analytical justification using generalized spin echo and quasiperiodic SU(2) cocycles; numerical study of integrability-breaking perturbations.
AI.result: Self-similar quantum revivals are observed in fidelity and entanglement entropy. The dynamics between revivals supports tunable volume-law or area-law entanglement scaling. Under integrability-breaking perturbations, a prethermal regime with algebraically tunable lifetime occurs before heating dominates.
AI.conclusion: Self-similar quantum revivals represent a new paradigm for nonequilibrium quantum matter, with realistic prospects for observation in current quantum simulators.

title: Isospectrality and Operator Complexity
summary: We study a pair of exactly solvable, isospectral fermion chains, one strongly interacting and one quadratic, that nevertheless display remarkably different phase structures and operator dynamics. A nonlocal nonlinear unitary transformation maps one onto the other while preserving the entire many-body spectrum and converting local fermion operators into extended many-body strings. Thus, operators that evolve within a closed linear subspace in the quadratic model become interacting operators that generate increasingly higher-body terms and exhibit asymptotic Lanczos growth $b_n\propto\sqrt n$. Despite their identical spectra, the two models realize distinct phases and sharply different notions of operator complexity. Our results demonstrate that free many-body spectra and interacting operator dynamics are fundamentally compatible.

AI.tldr: Two isospectral fermion chains (one strongly interacting, one quadratic) connected by a nonlocal unitary transformation exhibit identical spectra but distinct phase structures and operator dynamics, with the interacting model showing asymptotic Lanczos growth $b_n\propto\sqrt n$ despite being spectrally free.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether identical many-body spectra can coexist with fundamentally different operator dynamics and phase structures, challenging the conventional link between spectral properties and complexity.
AI.method: Study a pair of exactly solvable, isospectral fermion chains connected by a nonlocal nonlinear unitary transformation; analyze operator dynamics via Lanczos coefficients and many-body string growth.
AI.result: The interacting model exhibits asymptotic Lanczos growth $b_n\propto\sqrt n$ characteristic of chaotic systems, while the quadratic model yields linear subspace evolution; identical spectra nonetheless yield sharply different notions of operator complexity.
AI.conclusion: Free many-body spectra and interacting operator dynamics are fundamentally compatible; spectral isospectrality does not imply equivalence of dynamical or phase structure.

title: Continuous-variable ADAPT-VQE for bosonic lattice models
summary: We present a continuous-variable adaptive variational quantum eigensolver (CV-ADAPT-VQE). As concrete examples, we consider the ground-state preparation for (i) the Bose-Hubbard model and (ii) the bosonic Kitaev chain, including its extension with an on-site Kerr interaction. The former conserves the total boson number, while the latter conserves global parity. We construct symmetry-preserving operator pools tailored to each case and show, using GPU-based classical simulations, that CV-ADAPT-VQE results in significantly shallower circuits compared to Hamiltonian-based VQE approaches. Our results point toward direct applications in quantum simulations of condensed-matter systems, quantum chemistry, and high-energy physics.

AI.tldr: A continuous-variable adaptive variational quantum eigensolver (CV-ADAPT-VQE) is presented for ground-state preparation of bosonic systems, using symmetry-preserving operator pools to achieve significantly shallower circuits than Hamiltonian-based VQE approaches.
AI.motivation: To develop efficient quantum algorithms for bosonic systems (Bose-Hubbard model, bosonic Kitaev chain) that conserve symmetries (boson number, parity) and reduce circuit depth compared to standard Hamiltonian-based VQE methods.
AI.method: The CV-ADAPT-VQE algorithm adaptively builds ansatz circuits by selecting operators from symmetry-preserving pools tailored to each system (number-conserving for Bose-Hubbard, parity-conserving for Kitaev chain). Classical GPU simulations are used to benchmark circuit depth.
AI.result: CV-ADAPT-VQE produces significantly shallower circuits than Hamiltonian-based VQE approaches for both the Bose-Hubbard model and the bosonic Kitaev chain (including with Kerr interaction).
AI.conclusion: The method is promising for quantum simulations of condensed-matter systems, quantum chemistry, and high-energy physics.

title: Setting angles in quantum approximate optimization at utility-scale
summary: The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is a powerful heuristic that seeks to solve combinatorial optimization problems using quantum hardware and classical optimization in tandem. Various methods exist to train the parameterized quantum circuits that serve as an ansatz in QAOA. However, which method works best to identify optimal angles for a given problem instance remains poorly understood, especially at utility-scale, i.e., $100$ qubits or more. In this work, we address this challenge through utility-scale benchmarks from which we distill operational guidance for QAOA practitioners. First, we investigate approximation techniques, such as matrix product states and Pauli propagation, to find optimal angles. Second, we train QAOA on small-scale representative problems and transfer the angles to larger ones. We then validate the results on quantum hardware for utility-scale problem instances that can be meaningfully executed. In this way, we identify insights for QAOA angle setting strategies that work best for problems at the utility scale, including as a function of resource cost for the search. Crucially, the operational implications we draw from our benchmarks will help quantum optimization practitioners execute QAOA end-to-end pipelines efficiently on current and future hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks methods for training QAOA at utility scale (≥100 qubits), investigating approximation techniques (matrix product states, Pauli propagation) and angle transfer from small to large problems, providing operational guidance for practitioners executing QAOA on quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: The training of parameterized quantum circuits in QAOA is poorly understood at utility scale (100+ qubits), and no clear guidance exists on which angle-setting strategies work best for large problem instances.
AI.method: The authors benchmark approximation techniques (matrix product states, Pauli propagation) for finding optimal angles, and test angle transfer from small-scale to utility-scale problems, validating results on quantum hardware.
AI.result: They identify which QAOA angle-setting strategies work best at utility scale as a function of resource cost, and distill operational insights from their benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The operational implications drawn from utility-scale benchmarks will help quantum optimization practitioners execute QAOA end-to-end pipelines efficiently on current and future hardware.

title: Feature Encoding in Quantum Machine Learning: A Survey and Practical Guidelines
comment: Article submitted to ACM Computer Surveys the 15-Apr-2026
summary: The encoding of classical data into quantum states constitutes the primary performance bottleneck in Quantum Machine Learning (qml) on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (nisq) devices. No existing framework jointly characterises resource cost, expressivity, and noise robustness, nor provides actionable selection guidelines for practitioners. This survey addresses that gap through a systematic review of 66 primary works (2017-2026) assembled via a PRISMA-adapted protocol across five academic databases. Four principal contributions are made. First, a three-axis cost-expressivity-robustness taxonomy classifies all major encoding families - basis, angle, dense-angle, amplitude, data re-uploading, and IQP - along independently measurable axes. Second, closed-form depth-fidelity bounds under nisq decoherence channels identify the critical gate-error rate p* ~ 10^-3 below which amplitude encoding is viable. Third, a unified treatment of Fourier expressivity, barren-plateau onset, and quantum kernel concentration as functions of the encoding circuit provides the first joint trainability analysis. Fourth, a five-regime decision framework maps (D, n, p, tau) - feature dimension, qubit budget, error rate, and task type - to a hardware-grounded encoding recommendation. The central finding is that for p >= 10^-3, shallow angle-based encodings consistently outperform amplitude encoding in practice, despite the latter's exponential qubit advantage.

AI.tldr: This survey of 66 papers (2017-2026) proposes a three-axis cost-expressivity-robustness taxonomy for quantum encoding in QML, derives closed-form depth-fidelity bounds under NISQ noise (identifying p* ~ 10^-3 as the critical gate-error threshold for amplitude encoding viability), provides a unified trainability analysis linking Fourier expressivity, barren plateaus, and kernel concentration, and offers a five-regime decision framework mapping (D, n, p, τ) to hardware-grounded encoding recommendations. The key practical finding: for p ≥ 10^-3, shallow angle-based encodings outperform amplitude encoding despite the latter's exponential qubit advantage.
AI.motivation: Existing frameworks fail to jointly characterize resource cost, expressivity, and noise robustness for quantum encodings in QML on NISQ devices, leaving practitioners without actionable selection guidelines.
AI.method: Systematic literature review of 66 primary works (2017-2026) via a PRISMA-adapted protocol across five academic databases, followed by taxonomic classification, theoretical bound derivation, and unified trainability analysis.
AI.result: A three-axis taxonomy of encoding families; closed-form depth-fidelity bounds under NISQ decoherence identifying critical gate-error rate p* ~ 10^-3; first joint analysis of Fourier expressivity, barren-plateau onset, and kernel concentration; and a five-regime decision framework mapping (D, n, p, τ) to encoding recommendations.
AI.conclusion: For noise levels p ≥ 10^-3, shallow angle-based encodings are practically superior to amplitude encoding, despite amplitude encoding's exponential qubit efficiency.

title: Multi-Qubit Dyadic Phase Fixing for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Compilation
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires translating application-level quantum circuits into the Clifford+$T$ gate set, where the $T$ gate is the dominant resource cost. Phase kickback is an ancilla-based technique that can dramatically reduce $T$-count for rotations with dyadic angles, but has previously been limited to highly structured circuit families. We present Dyadic Phase Fixing (DPF), a general multi-qubit synthesis tool that extends phase kickback to general quantum circuits. DPF uses numerical unitary synthesis to greedily extract dyadic angle rotations from any input circuit. Combined with a decision matrix to automatically size the final phase gradient register, our end-to-end workflow achieves up to 70% reduction in $T$-count compared to \texttt{gridsynth} and up to 60% compared to Repeat-Until-Success synthesis on a diverse set of benchmarks. We map these compiled circuits to a surface-code architecture to evaluate space-time volume, demonstrating up to a 60\% reduction in this metric as well. However, for some circuits and mapping strategies the two metrics diverge significantly, demonstrating that $T$-count alone is a useful but incomplete proxy for fault-tolerant program costs.

AI.tldr: DPF extends phase kickback to general quantum circuits via numerical unitary synthesis, achieving up to 70% T-count reduction and 60% space-time volume reduction over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Phase kickback reduces T-count for dyadic rotations but was limited to structured circuits; a general synthesis tool was needed to extend these benefits to arbitrary quantum circuits.
AI.method: DPF greedily extracts dyadic angle rotations using numerical unitary synthesis, combined with a decision matrix for automatic phase gradient register sizing.
AI.result: Up to 70% T-count reduction vs. gridsynth, up to 60% vs. Repeat-Until-Success; up to 60% space-time volume reduction on surface-code architecture; T-count and space-time volume diverge for some circuits.
AI.conclusion: DPF is an effective general synthesis tool for reducing T-count, but T-count alone is an incomplete proxy for fault-tolerant costs.

title: On the Cryptographic Structure Required for Verifying Qubits
summary:
Classically testing for the presence of anti-commuting operators on a quantum device is a critical tool underpinning recent progress in classical verification of quantum computation. While such tests can be based on cryptographic assumptions, known constructions rely on highly structured assumptions, e.g. trapdoor claw-free functions.
  In this work, we seek to explain this state of affairs by constructing strong cryptography from (certain forms of) classical tests of anti-commutation. In particular, we formulate the notion of a test of non-commutation (ToNC), an interactive protocol between a quantum prover and classical verifier in which the prover's final-round response is obtained by measuring one of two binary observables $P_0,P_1$ depending on the verifier's challenge bit $c$. We prove that, for a broad range of parameters, ToNC implies classical-communication key agreement (KA), and ToNC combined with one-way functions implies oblivious transfer (OT).
  Along the way, we develop tools for and provide the first known results on hardness amplification for post-quantum KA and OT, where communication is classical but adversaries may be quantum. In particular, we prove the following results of independent interest.
  - Post-quantum hard-core measure theorem: For any efficiently sampleable high-min-entropy distribution $D$ over pairs $(x,b)$ such that quantum circuits have advantage at most $δ$ in predicting $b$ from $x$, there exists a sub-distribution $M\preceq D$ of density $(1-δ)$ on which $b$ is nearly optimally quantum-hard to predict.
  - Post-quantum interactive XOR lemma: Given any classically-interactive protocol, if quantum adversaries have advantage at most $δ$ in guessing a private challenger bit $b$, then two sequential repetitions reduce the advantage for predicting the XOR of the challenger bits $b_1\oplus b_2$ to at most $δ^2+\rm{negl}(λ)$.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that classical tests of anti-commutation (ToNC) imply key agreement (KA) and, combined with one-way functions, oblivious transfer (OT). It also develops the first hardness amplification results for post-quantum KA and OT, including a post-quantum hard-core measure theorem and a post-quantum interactive XOR lemma.
AI.motivation: To explain why existing classical verification tests for anti-commuting operators rely on highly structured cryptographic assumptions (e.g., trapdoor claw-free functions), by showing that such tests inherently imply strong cryptography (KA and OT).
AI.method: Formalizes the notion of a Test of Non-Commutation (ToNC), an interactive protocol where a quantum prover responds to a classical verifier's challenge bit by measuring one of two binary observables. Proves that ToNC implies classical-communication key agreement, and ToNC + one-way functions implies oblivious transfer. Develops two new technical tools: a post-quantum hard-core measure theorem and a post-quantum interactive XOR lemma.
AI.result: ToNC (for a broad parameter range) implies key agreement; ToNC plus one-way functions implies oblivious transfer. Additionally, the post-quantum hard-core measure theorem shows that any efficiently sampleable distribution with bounded quantum prediction advantage contains a dense sub-distribution where prediction is nearly impossible. The interactive XOR lemma shows that two sequential repetitions reduce guessing advantage from δ to δ² + negligible.
AI.conclusion: Classical tests of anti-commutation are inherently cryptographic primitives, explaining why they require structured assumptions. The new hardness amplification results are of independent interest for post-quantum cryptography.

title: A Class of Multipartite Entangled States Based on State Transitions
summary: We introduce Transition states (T states), denoted by $\ket{T_k^n}$, as a class of multipartite entangled states characterized by a fixed number of state transitions between adjacent qubits. These states form equal-amplitude superpositions over all states with a specified transition count. Unlike Bell states based on two-qubit correlations, GHZ states characterized by global correlations among all qubits, and W and Dicke states based on fixed numbers of qubit excitations, T states are defined by transition counts along an ordered sequence of qubits. We prove that T states are unitarily equivalent to Dicke states through a chain of CX (controlled-X) operations, thereby establishing a direct correspondence between transition-based and excitation-based representations of multipartite entanglement.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Transition states (T states) as a new class of multipartite entangled states defined by transition counts between adjacent qubits, proving they are unitarily equivalent to Dicke states via CX operations.
AI.motivation: To define a new class of multipartite entangled states based on transition counts between adjacent qubits, distinct from existing entanglement families (Bell, GHZ, W, Dicke).
AI.method: Defines T states $\ket{T_k^n}$ as equal-amplitude superpositions over states with a fixed number of transitions. Establishes unitary equivalence to Dicke states via a chain of CX (controlled-X) operations.
AI.result: T states are unitarily equivalent to Dicke states, establishing a direct correspondence between transition-based and excitation-based representations of multipartite entanglement.
AI.conclusion: T states offer a novel, transition-count-based perspective on multipartite entanglement, with proven structural connection to the well-studied Dicke states.

title: Quantum Radar Cross Section with two-photon entangled states
summary: We study two-photon entangled states for quantum radar cross section (QRCS), which is an extension of a single-photon QRCS formula. Since signal-idler entanglement does not provide any enhancement of the QRCS [Brandsema's PhD Thesis (2017)], we focus on signal-signal entanglement and derive the corresponding biphoton QRCS. We show that it can provide an enhancement over the single-photon QRCS and two-photon separable QRCS, where the performance is evaluated for various two-dimensional target geometries in monostatic/bistatic configurations. Furthermore, using the double-Gaussian approximation, we derive QRCS formula for biphoton states with arbitrary degree of entanglement and compute the resulting scattering patterns.

AI.tldr: This paper studies biphoton (signal-signal) entangled states for quantum radar cross section (QRCS), deriving formulas that show enhancement over single-photon and two-photon separable QRCS for various 2D target geometries in monostatic/bistatic configurations, and using a double-Gaussian approximation to compute scattering patterns for arbitrary entanglement degrees.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether entangled photon states can provide enhancement in quantum radar cross section (QRCS), motivated by the fact that signal-idler entanglement was previously shown to not provide any QRCS enhancement.
AI.method: Derives biphoton QRCS formula for signal-signal entanglement, evaluates performance for various 2D target geometries in monostatic/bistatic configurations, and uses double-Gaussian approximation to derive QRCS formula for biphoton states with arbitrary degree of entanglement.
AI.result: Signal-signal biphoton entanglement can provide an enhancement over both single-photon QRCS and two-photon separable QRCS.
AI.conclusion: Signal-signal entanglement offers a genuine advantage for quantum radar cross section, unlike signal-idler entanglement, and the derived formulas enable characterization of scattering patterns across varying entanglement degrees.

title: Decoder-Consistent Hamiltonians for POVM-Based Quantum Relaxations
summary: In compression-based quantum relaxations like QRAO, classical variables are encoded into qubits and decoded after optimization. We formalize that the choice of the quantum Hamiltonian is fundamentally determined by this decoder. By representing the decoder as a POVM, we define a unique decoder-consistent Hamiltonian via the pullback of the post-decoding expected objective value. Using this framework, we reveal that standard QRAO Hamiltonians are inconsistent for certain mixed-degree quadratic functions, and we provide new approximation guarantees for the MaxCut problem based directly on POVM decoder design.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes the relationship between quantum Hamiltonian design and decoder choice in compression-based quantum relaxations (QRAO), revealing inconsistencies in standard Hamiltonians for mixed-degree quadratic functions and providing new MaxCut approximation guarantees based on POVM decoder design.
AI.motivation: To formalize the fundamental relationship between quantum Hamiltonian choice and decoder design in quantum relaxation optimization (QRAO), and to resolve inconsistencies in existing approaches.
AI.method: Represents decoder as a POVM, defines decoder-consistent Hamiltonian via pullback of post-decoding expected objective value, and analyzes standard QRAO Hamiltonians within this framework.
AI.result: Reveals that standard QRAO Hamiltonians are inconsistent for certain mixed-degree quadratic functions, and provides new approximation guarantees for the MaxCut problem based on POVM decoder design.
AI.conclusion: The choice of quantum Hamiltonian is fundamentally determined by the decoder; using the POVM framework reveals inconsistencies in standard approaches and enables provably better approximations for MaxCut.

title: Gauging the Spacetime Code
summary: In recent years, the spacetime code has arisen as a candidate for a unifying view of fault tolerance in space and time. On the other hand, the recent study of dynamical phases has increasingly turned its attention to fault tolerance as a notion of a dynamically stable process. In this work, I explore one pathway between the two, achieved by gauging the spacetime code. This gives rise to a lattice gauge theory that inherits the elements of fault tolerance associated with a circuit, with Gauss laws corresponding to equivalence relations between configurations of spacetime errors and Wilson loops corresponding to detectors. The obtained gauge theory finds a surprisingly wide array of applications, from quantum error correction to condensed matter physics, and even learning theory: (1) It contains in its description foliated computation, and hence gives rise to one version of a gauge theory for measurement-based quantum computation. (2) For a class of topologically ordered mixed states, it gives us a gauge-theoretic language to describe the classical memory associated with the state. (3) The gauge-invariant observables of the theory which describe detectors also coincide with the learnable degrees of freedom of circuit Pauli noise.

AI.tldr: This paper explores a connection between spacetime codes and fault tolerance by gauging the spacetime code, producing a lattice gauge theory where Gauss laws correspond to error equivalence relations and Wilson loops correspond to detectors. This gauge theory unifies concepts across quantum error correction, condensed matter physics, and learning theory, including foliated computation, topological memory in mixed states, and learnable noise degrees of freedom.
AI.motivation: To bridge two perspectives on fault tolerance—spacetime codes (unifying space and time) and dynamical phases (fault tolerance as dynamical stability)—by developing a gauge-theoretic framework that reveals deep structural connections between them.
AI.method: Gauging the spacetime code to construct a lattice gauge theory, where Gauss laws encode error equivalence relations and Wilson loops represent detectors.
AI.result: The gauge theory yields three key applications: (1) describing foliated computation and measurement-based quantum computation, (2) characterizing classical memory in topologically ordered mixed states, and (3) identifying gauge-invariant observables (detectors) with learnable degrees of freedom in circuit Pauli noise.
AI.conclusion: The gauged spacetime code provides a unifying theoretical framework that connects quantum error correction, condensed matter physics, and learning theory through a common gauge-theoretic language, revealing that fault tolerance, topological order, and learnability are interrelated concepts.

title: Learning Hamiltonians at Long Times
summary: We study the problem of learning an unknown $n$-qubit Hamiltonian $H$ from $U = e^{-iHt}$ for a single time $t$, where $t$ may be arbitrarily large. For broad families of local Hamiltonians, we prove that, with high probability over $H$ and $t$, any sum of local observables $A$ that is normalized and orthogonal to $H$ satisfies $\tfrac{1}{2^n}\|[U(t),A]\|_F^2 \geq 1/\text{poly}(n)$. The Hamiltonian is therefore the unique approximately conserved local observable, and we can efficiently recover $H$, up to scale, as the approximate null vector of a data matrix built from random product-state inputs and classical shadows. As a corollary, we obtain a weak equilibration statement: the infinite-temperature autocorrelation of every sum of local observables orthogonal to $H$ decays by at least an inverse-polynomial amount.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that for broad families of local Hamiltonians, any normalized local observable orthogonal to $H$ has $\frac{1}{2^n}\|[U(t),A]\|_F^2 \geq 1/\text{poly}(n)$, enabling efficient Hamiltonian recovery via classical shadows and random product states, with a corollary on weak equilibration.
AI.motivation: To study learning an unknown $n$-qubit Hamiltonian $H$ from a single time-evolution operator $U=e^{-iHt}$ for arbitrarily large $t$, and to establish that $H$ is the unique approximately conserved local observable.
AI.method: The paper proves a lower bound on the squared Frobenius commutator norm $\frac{1}{2^n}\|[U(t),A]\|_F^2$ for normalized local observables $A$ orthogonal to $H$, using random Hamiltonian ensembles and classical shadows from random product-state inputs to build a data matrix whose approximate null vector recovers $H$.
AI.result: With high probability over $H$ and $t$, any sum of local observables $A$ normalized and orthogonal to $H$ satisfies $\frac{1}{2^n}\|[U(t),A]\|_F^2 \geq 1/\text{poly}(n)$, and $H$ can be efficiently recovered up to scale as the approximate null vector of a data matrix.
AI.conclusion: $H$ is the unique approximately conserved local observable, enabling efficient Hamiltonian learning; as a corollary, the infinite-temperature autocorrelation of any sum of local observables orthogonal to $H$ decays by at least an inverse-polynomial amount, establishing a weak equilibration result.

title: Information-Geometric Bound on the Robustness of Entanglement Generation
summary: Entanglement generation is a central resource for quantum information processing, quantum networking, and quantum sensing. In practical implementations, however, entangling interactions are inevitably subject to uncertainty and fluctuations in the interaction strength. We investigate the robustness of entanglement generation in the presence of such imperfections and establish a direct connection between the robustness of entanglement generation and quantum Fisher information (QFI). For two interacting qubits, we show that the reduction in concurrence caused by fluctuations in the interaction parameter is bounded by the QFI with respect to the interaction strength.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how entanglement generation between two qubits is affected by fluctuations in interaction strength, and establishes a bound relating the reduction in concurrence to the quantum Fisher information (QFI) with respect to the interaction parameter.
AI.motivation: Entanglement is a key resource for quantum information processing, but practical implementations suffer from uncertainty in interaction strength, motivating the need to understand robustness against such imperfections.
AI.method: The authors analyze two interacting qubits and derive a theoretical bound connecting the reduction in concurrence (a measure of entanglement) caused by interaction-strength fluctuations to the quantum Fisher information with respect to the interaction parameter.
AI.result: The reduction in concurrence due to fluctuations in the interaction parameter is bounded by the quantum Fisher information with respect to that interaction strength.
AI.conclusion: There is a direct quantitative link between the robustness of entanglement generation and the quantum Fisher information, providing a fundamental bound on how interaction uncertainties degrade entanglement.

title: Symmetries and overparametrization properties of Hamiltonian variational ansatzes for the $(1+1)$d $\mathbb{Z}_2$ lattice gauge theory
summary: We perform detailed studies of five Hamiltonian variational ansatzes (HVA) based on the Hamiltonian of the $(1+1)$d $\mathbb{Z}_2$ lattice gauge theory. The ansatzes are designed to respect local and global symmetries of the original Hamiltonian and therefore act on a finely segmented state Hilbert space. Following Larocca et al. (2023), we numerically study the dimension of the dynamical Lie algebra (DLA) and the rank of the quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) of the ansatzes within specific invariant subspaces. The ansatzes all involve sums of weight-three Paulis in their generators, which is a feature that have so far been underexplored in this context. We also perform numerical experiments to determine the ground state energy of the original Hamiltonian via variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), and observe that overparametrization of the ansatzes coincides with the apparent disappearance of local minima in the loss function, in line with the finding in the reference. Finally, the decay rate of the VQE loss function under gradient descent optimization is revealed to scale linearly with the number of parameters in the ansatz. These results help to enrich the theory of overparameterization of quantum circuits and inform the design of scalable variational ansatzes.

AI.tldr: This paper studies five Hamiltonian variational ansatzes (HVA) for (1+1)d Z₂ lattice gauge theory, analyzing their dynamical Lie algebra dimensions, quantum Fisher information matrix ranks, and overparameterization in VQE for ground state energy estimation.
AI.motivation: To understand the overparameterization of quantum circuits and inform the design of scalable variational ansatzes respecting local and global symmetries, particularly focusing on weight-three Pauli generators which have been underexplored.
AI.method: Five HVA ansatzes are designed with local/global symmetry constraints. The study numerically computes DLA dimensions and QFIM ranks within invariant subspaces, performs VQE for ground state energy, and analyzes gradient descent loss function decay.
AI.result: Overparameterization coincides with disappearance of local minima in the loss function; the VQE loss function decay rate scales linearly with the number of parameters in the ansatz.
AI.conclusion: These results enrich the theory of overparameterization in quantum circuits and provide guidance for designing scalable variational ansatzes.

title: Optimal convex approximation of quantum channels based on $α$-affinity
summary: Determining the minimal distance between a target channel and a convex hull of predefined set of implementable channels is a fundamental problem in quantum resource theory, and provides key guidance for experimental implementations. In this work, we develop a unified analytical framework for optimal convex approximation of quantum channels based on the quantum $α$-affinity measure. We construct a channel distance metric induced by the α-affinity and the ChoiJamiolkowski isomorphism, which satisfies the required properties of a well-defined channel distance. Subsequently, we present an optimization framework for the convex approximation of quantum channels, and derive analytical solutions for the optimal convex approximation of single-qubit unitary channels over both the SU(2)-covariant and Pauli channel families, obtaining closed-form expressions for the optimal parameters and the minimal approximation distance. This framework is further applied to the amplitude-damping channel, yielding the explicit form of its optimal approximation and the associated minimal α-affinity distance. In contrast to conventional approaches based on the diamond norm, our framework provides a systematic and analytically tractable approach to quantum channel approximation under realistic constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a unified analytical framework for optimal convex approximation of quantum channels using the quantum α-affinity measure, deriving closed-form solutions for single-qubit unitary channels over SU(2)-covariant and Pauli channel families, and applying it to the amplitude-damping channel.
AI.motivation: Determining the minimal distance between a target channel and a convex hull of implementable channels is fundamental in quantum resource theory and essential for guiding experimental implementations.
AI.method: The authors construct a channel distance metric based on the α-affinity and Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism, then develop an optimization framework for convex approximation of quantum channels, deriving analytical solutions for single-qubit unitary channels over SU(2)-covariant and Pauli channel families.
AI.result: Closed-form expressions for optimal parameters and minimal approximation distance are obtained for single-qubit unitary channels. The framework is also applied to the amplitude-damping channel, yielding its explicit optimal approximation and minimal α-affinity distance.
AI.conclusion: Compared to diamond norm approaches, this framework provides a systematic and analytically tractable method for quantum channel approximation under realistic constraints.

title: Tight relation between the physical effects of a quantum measurement and the information gained about an observable
summary: The dynamics of quantum measurements defines a precise relation between the information gained about one physical property of a system and the observable changes in another physical property of the same system. Here, we express this relation in terms of the Hilbert space superpositions of the corresponding eigenstates and show how the probability of an observable physical change can be obtained from the Bayesian update of the probabilities associated with the information obtained in the measurement. Our analysis demonstrates that the superposition principle provides the tightest possible expression of the trade-off between information and back action in a quantum measurement.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a precise relationship between information gain and back action in quantum measurements, expressed via Hilbert space superpositions and Bayesian probability updates, showing that the superposition principle provides the tightest possible trade-off between information and observable physical changes.
AI.motivation: To formally express the fundamental trade-off between the information gained about one physical property and the observable changes induced in another property during quantum measurements, and to demonstrate that this relation is fundamentally constrained by the superposition principle.
AI.method: The authors express the measurement-induced dynamics in terms of Hilbert space superpositions of eigenstates and derive the probability of observable physical changes from Bayesian updates of measurement outcome probabilities.
AI.result: The superposition principle yields the tightest possible expression of the information-back action trade-off in quantum measurements.
AI.conclusion: The trade-off between information gain and back action in quantum measurements is fundamentally bounded by the superposition principle, establishing a precise quantitative relation between the two.

title: Periodic Symmetry-Adapted Encoding: Qubit Reduction in Crystalline Electronic Structure
summary: We extend the symmetry-adapted encoding (SAE) framework to periodic electronic structure, enabling qubit-efficient quantum simulation of crystalline materials. By constructing a $Γ$-point supercell Hamiltonian from a folded $k$-point calculation and systematically identifying all applicable space-group symmetry generators -- including spin-parity, point-group, and crystal translation symmetries -- we obtain qubit Hamiltonians with fewer qubits than the Jordan--Wigner starting point. We benchmark diamond, silicon, 3C-SiC, MgO, NaCl, CsCl, h-BN, wurtzite AlN, $α$-quartz SiO$_2$, and MgF$_2$ using active spaces chosen to preserve complete near-degenerate frontier manifolds across cubic, hexagonal, trigonal, and tetragonal space groups. Across the suite the periodic SAE removes 4--8 qubits. The B2 CsCl benchmark realises eight independent Boolean generators, i.e. a symmetry group isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}_2^8$, reducing CAS(6,7) from 14 to 6 qubits. This exceeds the $\mathbb{Z}_2^5$ maximum of molecular SAE, where only two spin parities and at most three independent Boolean point-group generators are available, because the folded crystal supplies three additional half-translation symmetries. Noiseless UCCSD-VQE benchmarks against exact diagonalisation in the active-space sector show that the reduced encodings preserve the target energies to well below chemical accuracy while reducing variational parameter counts by $3$--$8\times$ and CNOT counts by up to $309\times$. The largest circuit savings occur when translation and point-group generators act independently in the active space, demonstrating that periodic symmetry can be converted directly into both qubit and ansatz compression. The method is implemented in the open-source QuantumSymmetry package and requires no manual specification of symmetry generators.

AI.tldr: The paper extends symmetry-adapted encoding (SAE) to periodic systems, enabling qubit-efficient quantum simulation of crystals by leveraging space-group symmetries (including translation, point-group, and spin-parity). It benchmarks 10 materials, achieving up to 8-qubit reduction (e.g., CsCl: 14→6 qubits), 3–8× fewer variational parameters, and up to 309× CNOT reduction while preserving chemical accuracy. The method is automated in the open-source QuantumSymmetry package.
AI.motivation: To reduce qubit and circuit resource requirements for quantum simulations of periodic crystalline materials by exploiting space-group symmetries beyond what molecular SAE can achieve.
AI.method: Extends SAE to periodic systems by constructing a Γ-point supercell Hamiltonian from folded k-point calculations, identifying all applicable space-group symmetry generators (spin-parity, point-group, crystal translations), and encoding them as Boolean generators to reduce qubit count via symmetry-adapted qubit Hamiltonians.
AI.result: Across 10 materials (diamond, Si, 3C-SiC, MgO, NaCl, CsCl, h-BN, w-AlN, α-quartz SiO₂, MgF₂), periodic SAE removes 4–8 qubits. CsCl achieves 8 independent Boolean generators (ℤ₂⁸), reducing CAS(6,7) from 14 to 6 qubits. UCCSD-VQE benchmarks show <chemical accuracy, 3–8× fewer parameters, and up to 309× CNOT reduction.
AI.conclusion: Periodic symmetry can be directly converted into qubit and ansatz compression, with the largest circuit savings occurring when translation and point-group generators act independently in the active space. The method is fully automated and open-source.

title: Engineered dissipation for faster adiabatic state preparation
summary: Adiabatic state preparation is often slowed by nonadiabatic leakage near small spectral gaps. We propose an engineered dissipative protocol that uses a filtered reservoir to induce predominantly downward transitions in the instantaneous energy eigenbasis while leaving the instantaneous ground state dark. The leaked population generated by nonadiabatic driving is therefore continuously relaxed back toward the low-energy sector. An effective avoided-crossing analysis shows that in the regime where the engineered relaxation strength is much larger than the minimum gap, the runtime scaling can improve from the closed-system behavior $\mathcal{O}(Δ^{-2})$ to $\mathcal{O}(Δ^{-1})$ Finite-temperature upward transitions introduce a thermal error floor, but the enhancement survives when this heating rate remains below the target error tolerance. Numerical results show improved ground-state preparation over closed-system annealing. We also discuss a possible superconducting-circuit implementation using structured bosonic reservoirs.

AI.tldr: A dissipative protocol using a filtered reservoir to suppress nonadiabatic leakage in adiabatic state preparation, improving runtime scaling from O(Δ⁻²) to O(Δ⁻¹) and demonstrating improved ground-state preparation with a potential superconducting-circuit implementation.
AI.motivation: Adiabatic state preparation suffers from nonadiabatic leakage near small spectral gaps, which slows down the process. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by engineering a dissipative mechanism that continuously relaxes leaked population back to the low-energy sector.
AI.method: The protocol introduces a filtered reservoir that induces predominantly downward transitions in the instantaneous energy eigenbasis while keeping the ground state dark. An effective avoided-crossing analysis is performed, and numerical simulations compare the dissipative protocol with closed-system annealing. A superconducting-circuit implementation using structured bosonic reservoirs is discussed.
AI.result: Runtime scaling improves from O(Δ⁻²) (closed-system) to O(Δ⁻¹) when engineered relaxation strength >> minimum gap. Finite-temperature upward transitions introduce a thermal error floor, but enhancement persists if heating rate stays below target error tolerance. Numerical results confirm improved ground-state preparation.
AI.conclusion: Engineered dissipation can effectively accelerate adiabatic state preparation by mitigating nonadiabatic leakage, with practical feasibility suggested via superconducting-circuit platforms.

title: Symmetry-adapted qubit encoding with complete active space and Bravyi--Kitaev mapping for quantum chemistry on a quantum computer
summary: We present a symmetry-adapted qubit encoding with complete active space (SAE-CAS) for quantum chemistry on fault-tolerant and near-term quantum processors. Building on exact-symmetry encodings, we extend symmetry-adapted mappings to approximate $Z$-symmetries corresponding to frozen-core and virtual orbitals, thereby reducing qubit requirements without significant loss of accuracy. We derive the mapping from the second-quantised Hamiltonian to active-space qubit Hamiltonians, prove its equivalence to the canonical CAS Hamiltonian with frozen-core and virtual-orbital projection, and integrate it with point-group and spin-parity symmetry encodings via affine Clifford transformations to maximise qubit reduction while preserving the target symmetry sector. The same framework also accommodates the Bravyi--Kitaev mapping, yielding an SAE-CAS-BK variant that is unitarily equivalent to SAE-CAS. Numerical benchmarking on nine small molecules using UCCSD and a hardware-efficient shifted-circular-alternating (HE-SCA) ansatz shows that SAE-CAS reduces qubit counts and Pauli-operator weight, yields shallower circuits with fewer parameters, and often accelerates VQE convergence; with HE-SCA it consistently reaches CAS reference energies in cases where JW-CAS does not converge within the tested budgets. We provide an open-source implementation in the Python package QuantumSymmetry. SAE-CAS offers a route to resource-efficient molecular simulations on fault-tolerant and near-term quantum processors.

AI.tldr: SAE-CAS is a symmetry-adapted qubit encoding for quantum chemistry that reduces qubit requirements and circuit depth by extending symmetry-adapted mappings to approximate Z-symmetries (frozen-core/virtual orbitals), achieving resource-efficient molecular simulations on near-term and fault-tolerant quantum processors.
AI.motivation: To reduce qubit requirements and circuit complexity in quantum chemistry simulations on quantum processors by extending symmetry-adapted encodings to handle frozen-core and virtual orbital approximations without significant loss of accuracy.
AI.method: Extends exact-symmetry encodings to approximate Z-symmetries (frozen-core/virtual orbitals); derives mapping from second-quantised to active-space qubit Hamiltonians; proves equivalence to canonical CAS Hamiltonian; integrates point-group and spin-parity symmetries via affine Clifford transformations; also accommodates Bravyi-Kitaev mapping (SAE-CAS-BK).
AI.result: Benchmarked on nine small molecules with UCCSD and HE-SCA ansatz: SAE-CAS reduces qubit counts, Pauli-operator weight, yields shallower circuits with fewer parameters, accelerates VQE convergence; with HE-SCA consistently reaches CAS reference energies where JW-CAS fails within budget.
AI.conclusion: SAE-CAS provides a resource-efficient route to molecular simulations on both fault-tolerant and near-term quantum processors, with open-source implementation in QuantumSymmetry Python package.

title: No-go theorems on simulating uncertainty principle's signatures
summary: Uncertainty principle, one of the most iconic features of quantum mechanics, was originally viewed as a fundamental limitation. Since the inception of quantum information science, researchers began to use it to achieve quantum advantages. To better understand the origin of these advantages, an essential question is: To what extent can the uncertainty principle's signatures be simulated by a single measurement? As a single measurement clearly cannot demonstrate the uncertainty principle, such a simulation, if exists, implies the claimed advantages may either stem from other quantum features, or just be reproducible in a less resourceful way. In this work, we report a series of noise-robust no-go theorems, showing that strong enough signatures of uncertainty principle cannot be simulated by a single measurement, even when assisted by quantum pre- or post-processing. This signature is modelled by complementary instruments. We completely characterise complementary instruments by a numerically feasible measure and show that they are necessary and sufficient resources for the advantage in an operational task that aims to unambiguously send classical information.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that strong signatures of the uncertainty principle cannot be simulated by a single measurement, even with quantum pre- or post-processing, and shows that complementary instruments are necessary and sufficient resources for advantages in unambiguous classical information transmission.
AI.motivation: To understand whether quantum advantages attributed to the uncertainty principle can be simulated by a single measurement, which would imply these advantages either stem from other quantum features or are reproducible with fewer resources.
AI.method: The authors develop noise-robust no-go theorems that characterize complementary instruments with a numerically feasible measure, showing they are both necessary and sufficient for advantages in an operational task.
AI.result: Strong signatures of the uncertainty principle cannot be simulated by a single measurement, even with quantum pre- or post-processing assistance. Complementary instruments are completely characterized as the essential resource.
AI.conclusion: The uncertainty principle's strong signatures are genuine quantum resources that require complementary measurements, not single measurements, establishing foundational limits on what can be simulated with fewer quantum resources.

title: Non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics of a memory-bearing open-system process
summary: We show the emergence of memory effects in the dynamics of a driven two-level system interacting with a composite environment, and analyze their influence on work, heat and entropy production. We further investigate how the interplay between driving, dissipation and memory effects, stemming from the finiteness of the environment, shapes the thermodynamic response of the system, thus providing insight into quantum thermodynamics beyond the Markovian approximation.

AI.tldr: Study of memory effects in a driven two-level system interacting with a composite environment, analyzing their impact on work, heat, and entropy production in quantum thermodynamics beyond the Markovian approximation.
AI.motivation: To understand how memory effects (non-Markovianity) arising from a finite, composite environment influence thermodynamic quantities in driven quantum systems, going beyond standard Markovian approximations.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of a driven two-level system coupled to a composite environment, examining the interplay between driving, dissipation, and memory effects due to finite environment size.
AI.result: Memory effects emerge from the finiteness of the environment and significantly shape work, heat, and entropy production in the driven two-level system.
AI.conclusion: The interplay of driving, dissipation, and non-Markovian memory effects is crucial for understanding quantum thermodynamics in realistic finite environments, providing insights beyond the Markovian approximation.

title: Broadband AC Magnetic Field Sensing via Continuous wave optically detected magnetic resonance with NV Centers in diamond
summary: The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond has attracted considerable attention as a highly sensitive quantum sensor that can operate at room temperature. In particular, continuous-wave optically detected magnetic resonance (CW-ODMR) is promising for a wide range of applications because of its simplicity. However, conventional AC magnetic-field sensing schemes based on CW-ODMR suffer from a limited detection bandwidth: the detectable frequency is either fixed by intrinsic physical parameters of the NV center or, even when tunable, restricted to a narrow range of only a few MHz. Here, we propose a broadband AC magnetometry scheme based on CW-ODMR with NV centers using microwave-driven dressed states.Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, we show that the proposed scheme enables the detection of AC magnetic fields with frequencies up to the order of 100 MHz, which has been difficult to achieve using conventional CW-ODMR-based methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a broadband AC magnetometry scheme using microwave-driven dressed states in NV centers, extending the detectable AC magnetic field frequency range to ~100 MHz via CW-ODMR, overcoming the narrow bandwidth limitation of conventional methods.
AI.motivation: Conventional CW-ODMR-based AC magnetic-field sensing has limited detection bandwidth: the detectable frequency is either fixed by intrinsic NV parameters or restricted to a narrow range (~few MHz). The authors aim to overcome this limitation.
AI.method: The authors propose a broadband AC magnetometry scheme based on CW-ODMR with NV centers using microwave-driven dressed states. They validate the approach through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations.
AI.result: The proposed scheme enables detection of AC magnetic fields with frequencies up to ~100 MHz, which was previously difficult to achieve with conventional CW-ODMR-based methods.
AI.conclusion: The microwave-driven dressed-state approach significantly broadens the detection bandwidth of CW-ODMR-based AC magnetometry, making it suitable for applications requiring higher-frequency AC field sensing while maintaining the simplicity of CW-ODMR.

title: Double-bracket quantum algorithms for thermal state preparation
summary: We propose quantum algorithms for preparing thermal states via the simulation of the thermofield double states. The key idea is to leverage double-bracket quantum algorithms to implement imaginary-time evolution on thermofield double states, whose reduced state realizes the Gibbs state. Our method, termed double-bracket thermofield double (DB-TFD), introduces two variants. The first, the vanilla DB-TFD algorithm, directly implements imaginary-time evolution using double-bracket quantum imaginary-time evolution. The second, poly DB-TFD, employs double-bracket quantum signal processing to approximate the imaginary-time evolution operator via a polynomial transformation. We demonstrate that the complexity of the poly DB-TFD algorithm scales exponentially with the inverse temperature in a broad practical regime. This scaling is consistent with existing methods, and numerical simulations support the corresponding theoretical bound. We further demonstrate the utility of DB-TFD in quantum Boltzmann machines for generative modeling, achieving improved performance compared with variational imaginary-time evolution approaches. These results establish DB-TFD as a promising route for thermal state preparation in the near-term and early-fault-tolerant regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes quantum algorithms (DB-TFD) for preparing thermal states by simulating thermofield double states using double-bracket quantum algorithms to implement imaginary-time evolution, with two variants (vanilla and poly DB-TFD), achieving exponential complexity scaling with inverse temperature and demonstrating improved performance in quantum Boltzmann machines for generative modeling.
AI.motivation: The goal is to develop efficient quantum algorithms for preparing thermal (Gibbs) states, which are essential for quantum statistical mechanics and applications like quantum Boltzmann machines, by leveraging the thermofield double formalism and double-bracket quantum algorithms.
AI.method: Two variants are introduced: (1) vanilla DB-TFD, which directly implements imaginary-time evolution using double-bracket quantum imaginary-time evolution, and (2) poly DB-TFD, which uses double-bracket quantum signal processing to approximate the imaginary-time evolution operator via polynomial transformation.
AI.result: The complexity of poly DB-TFD scales exponentially with inverse temperature in a broad practical regime, consistent with existing methods. Numerical simulations support the theoretical bound. DB-TFD achieves improved performance in quantum Boltzmann machines compared to variational imaginary-time evolution approaches.
AI.conclusion: DB-TFD is established as a promising route for thermal state preparation in near-term and early-fault-tolerant quantum regimes.

title: Magnetic flux as a quantized Lorentz pseudoscalar and its relation to electric charge quantization
summary: In this paper, we re-examine the well-known question of why electric charges exist only in quantized portions. In this context, we revisit the motion of a charged particle in a field-free region around a current-carrying solenoid. Solving the corresponding Schrödinger equation leads to a simultaneous quantization condition for the magnetic flux and the electric charge. We also demonstrate the Lorentz invariance of this condition by showing that the magnetic flux behaves like a pseudoscalar under Lorentz transformations.

AI.tldr: The paper re-examines charge quantization by analyzing a charged particle around a solenoid, deriving a simultaneous quantization condition for magnetic flux and electric charge, and showing its Lorentz invariance via the flux's pseudoscalar behavior.
AI.motivation: To re-examine the fundamental question of why electric charges exist only in quantized portions, which is a long-standing puzzle in physics.
AI.method: Solving the Schrödinger equation for a charged particle moving in a field-free region around a current-carrying solenoid, and analyzing Lorentz invariance of the resulting quantization condition by examining the transformation properties of magnetic flux as a pseudoscalar.
AI.result: A simultaneous quantization condition linking magnetic flux and electric charge is derived; the Lorentz invariance of this condition is demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: The quantization of electric charge is intimately connected to the quantization of magnetic flux, and this relationship is Lorentz invariant, providing a deeper understanding of charge quantization.

title: Shattering the Symmetry Trap in Fixed-Ansatz VQE: An Accelerated ADAPT-VQE Study of Three Pillar Molecules under Bravyi-Kitaev Mapping
comment: 8 pages, including raw algorithmic telemetry logs
summary: Fixed-ansatz Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQE), such as the Unitary Coupled Cluster with Singles and Doubles (UCCSD) framework, frequently suffer from severe initialization paralyzation and zero-gradient traps when evaluated using the non-local Bravyi-Kitaev (BK) fermion-to-qubit mapping. In this work, we systematically demonstrate how the Adaptive Derivative-Assembled Pseudo-Trotter (ADAPT-VQE) framework shatters these structural limitations across three distinct electronic and geometric molecular pillars: Lithium Hydride ($\text{LiH}$), Hydrogen Fluoride ($\text{HF}$), and Water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$), under heavily stretched or asymmetric multi-reference configurations. While conventional UCCSD-VQE flatlines completely at a zero energy shift ($0.000000$~Ha) due to global phase cancellations inherent to the BK tree structures, our dynamic ADAPT-VQE loop successfully isolates the dominant symmetry-breaking operators using analytical commutator gradients. To bypass the severe $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ computational bottlenecks of dense matrix exponentiation and Singular Value Decomposition on larger registers, we implement a highly optimized, vector-based Taylor series expansion state-evolution engine. Our numerical results show that the accelerated ADAPT-VQE framework achieves instant, exact Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) convergence within the very first macro-cycle across all three molecular systems, maintaining absolute numerical stability up to a 12-qubit register space. This study establishes a robust, hardware-efficient path for simulating strongly correlated, highly polarized triatomic chemical environments on near-term local architectures.

AI.tldr: ADAPT-VQE overcomes initialization paralyzation and zero-gradient traps in fixed-ansatz VQE (UCCSD) under BK mapping, achieving instant FCI convergence for LiH, HF, and H₂O in stretched/asymmetric configurations using a vector-based Taylor series evolution engine.
AI.motivation: Fixed-ansatz VQE (e.g., UCCSD) suffers from severe initialization paralyzation and zero-gradient traps when using the Bravyi-Kitaev fermion-to-qubit mapping, preventing convergence for strongly correlated molecular systems.
AI.method: ADAPT-VQE with analytical commutator gradients and a vector-based Taylor series expansion state-evolution engine (bypassing dense matrix exponentiation and SVD bottlenecks).
AI.result: Instant, exact FCI convergence within the first macro-cycle for LiH, HF, and H₂O; absolute numerical stability up to 12 qubits.
AI.conclusion: ADAPT-VQE provides a hardware-efficient path for simulating strongly correlated, highly polarized triatomic molecules on near-term quantum architectures.

title: Rapid Gaussian Boson Sampling Circuit Screening for GKP States Creation via a Two-Stage Machine Learning Surrogate
summary: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are essential non-Gaussian resources for fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, enabling logical qubit encoding with intrinsic robustness against errors. Several approaches to GKP state preparation have been explored, including measurement-based protocols in circuit QED and trapped-ion systems, cat-state breeding, and photon-subtraction schemes. However, these methods are either restricted to specific platforms or require deep non-Gaussian resource chains with exponentially low success probabilities. Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) offers a compelling all-photonic alternative by generating non-Gaussian states through measurement-induced nonlinearity, without the need for matter-based ancilla or active feedforward. Nevertheless, its practical implementation is limited by the exponential computational cost of evaluating matrix hafnians-#P-complete functions that govern photon-number probabilities. To address this challenge, we introduce a two-stage Histogram Gradient Boosting surrogate pipeline that predicts, without any hafnian computation, the optimal heralding pattern, circuit fidelity, and post-selection probability for candidate GBS circuits, while reserving exact quantum simulation exclusively for surrogate-selected candidates. Trained on circuit configurations across 3-5 optical modes, the surrogate achieves 90.0% GKP-detection accuracy on a held-out set, representing a 23.7 percentage-point improvement over the baseline, with a fidelity mean absolute error of 0.032 and a log-scale post-selection probability $R^2 = 0.837$, reducing the total simulation burden by approximately 90%.

AI.tldr: Introduces a Histogram Gradient Boosting surrogate pipeline to bypass computationally expensive hafnian calculations in GBS-based GKP state preparation, achieving 90% detection accuracy and ~90% reduction in simulation burden.
AI.motivation: Existing GKP state preparation methods are either platform-specific or require deep non-Gaussian resource chains with exponentially low success probabilities. GBS offers a promising alternative but is limited by the #P-complete computational cost of evaluating matrix hafnians.
AI.method: A two-stage Histogram Gradient Boosting surrogate pipeline that predicts optimal heralding pattern, circuit fidelity, and post-selection probability for GBS circuits without hafnian computation, reserving exact quantum simulation only for surrogate-selected candidates.
AI.result: 90.0% GKP-detection accuracy (23.7 pp improvement over baseline), fidelity MAE of 0.032, log-scale post-selection probability R²=0.837, and ~90% reduction in total simulation burden on 3-5 mode circuit configurations.
AI.conclusion: Machine learning surrogates can effectively bypass the #P-complete bottleneck in GBS-based GKP state preparation, making all-photonic fault-tolerant quantum computing more practically feasible.

title: Polymer quantum mechanics on compact configuration spaces
summary: "Polymer quantum mechanics" is the name given to a quantization scheme inspired by loop quantum gravity in which the configuration space of the theory is chosen to have a discrete topology. Polymer quantization yields a representation of the canonical commutation relations that is genuinely distinct from the conventional "Schrödinger" representation. In this paper, we summarize the main features of polymer quantum mechanics and investigate in detail the polymer quantization of systems with configuration spaces that are classically compact. We show explicitly how using the standard construction of polymer states leads to a Hilbert space of states defined on a finite graph of points. By way of example, we find the exact energy eigenvalues and eigenfunctions for a particle on a ring and a particle in a box defined on such lattices, and discuss similarities and differences from standard Schrödinger quantum mechanics. We also explore the continuum limit of states in these systems, and demonstrate in detail how the exact eigenfunctions in the position representation approach their continuum counterparts.

AI.tldr: This paper explores polymer quantum mechanics—a quantization scheme inspired by loop quantum gravity with discrete configuration spaces—applied to systems with compact classical configuration spaces (particle on a ring and particle in a box). It constructs Hilbert spaces on finite graphs, derives exact energy eigenvalues and eigenfunctions on such lattices, and analyzes the continuum limit where eigenfunctions converge to standard Schrödinger counterparts.
AI.motivation: To extend polymer quantization (a loop quantum gravity-inspired discrete approach) to systems with classically compact configuration spaces, and to understand how the standard construction of polymer states leads to Hilbert spaces on finite graphs, contrasting with conventional Schrödinger quantum mechanics.
AI.method: The authors apply the polymer quantization scheme to compact configuration spaces (particle on a ring and particle in a box) by constructing polymer states on finite graphs of points, solving for exact energy eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, and then analyzing the continuum limit by examining how lattice eigenfunctions approach their continuum Schrödinger counterparts.
AI.result: Exact energy eigenvalues and eigenfunctions are derived for a particle on a ring and a particle in a box under polymer quantization on finite lattices. The continuum limit is demonstrated in detail, showing convergence of polymer eigenfunctions to standard Schrödinger eigenfunctions in the position representation.
